l: the Judgment of Paris, Heroides and Amores
s: The Judgment of Paris is a beauty contest in which Jupiter’s messenger commands Paris to judge Venus, Juno, and Minerva/Pallas, who appear before him, reportedly naked, on Mount Ida. Juno offers kingdoms, Pallas valor, and Venus Helen. Paris accepts Venus’s promise, awards her victory, and the event is recalled as beginning a disastrous change in his love, though Helen doubts his account and the alleged prize.

l: Paris's departure from Oenone, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris’s departure is associated with tears, embraces, repeated kisses, and difficulty saying farewell. Oenone watches his sails leave, follows them with her eyes, and wets the sand with her tears.

l: Paris's return with Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris returns by ship with Helen, embracing her instead of returning for Oenone, whose grief and self-wounding fill Ida with lamentation.

l: love between Oenone and Paris, Heroides and Amores
s: Oenone and Paris’s pastoral love involved shared rural life, embraces, and tears; after Paris returned with Helen, he abandoned Oenone despite her wish to remain his wife.

Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas and granddaughter of Bacchus, possesses Lemnos as her marriage portion. She welcomed and married Jason, bore their twin sons, then writes reproaching his silence and marriage to Medea, asserting her lawful bond and wishing Medea similar suffering.

Jason, a Pagasaean Pelasgian and son of Aeson, sails to Colchis for the Golden Fleece. There he asks Medea’s magic to save him through the trials of Mars’s bulls, the earth-born men, and the dragon; he takes the Fleece and returns safely to Thessaly with Medea. He had promised to return to Hypsipyle, his wife and mother of his twin sons, but abandons them. Though he promises Medea marriage, he later orders her from his palace and marries Creusa.

Medea is a Colchian barbarian poisoner and powerful sorceress, daughter of Aeetes and sister of Chalciope and Absyrtus. Devoted to Jason, she uses drugs, incantations, herbs, and magic to save him from the fire-breathing bulls, armed warriors, and sleepless dragon. For him she betrays Aeetes, abandons her family and homeland, flees Colchis, and kills Absyrtus. She accompanies Jason and takes the marriage-bed promised to Hypsipyle, drawing condemnation for crime and enchantment. Jason then abandons and exiles her for Creusa, leaving her unable to return to her parents or sister, grieving and vengeful.
Mars, a god associated with warfare, hindered Dipsas’s young woman through a contrary star, then departed, leaving Venus favorably placed; it is involved in Venus and wields a sword against men.
Lemnos, fertile land and Hypsipyle’s homeland, survives its massacre through her rescue of her father and becomes part of her marriage portion to Jason.

is_homeland_of Medea [her native realm] Colchis is Medea's native land and the realm of her father, Aeetes. Jason and the Greek crew arrive there seeking the golden fleece, and Medea later leaves Colchis with Jason.

The Argo, the first ship to open sea routes, carries Jason and his companions from Lemnos after he boards last, while Hypsipyle watches it depart. It carries the Golden Fleece through the clashing rocks, becoming the first ship through that dangerous sea; a speaker wishes it had been overwhelmed.

l: the Golden Fleece, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a golden fleece [taken from the ram of Phrixus] Jason is reported to have taken the golden fleece from the ram of Phrixus, which had been guarded by an ever-watchful dragon. Hypsipyle questions whether Jason or Medea deserves the credit for obtaining it.

l: the golden ram, Heroides and Amores
s: The golden ram, remarkable for its deep fleece, carries Phrixus safely over the sea. Its golden fleece becomes an expedition’s prize, is obtained from a ploughed field, and is claimed as the speaker’s dowry, which her husband would refuse to return.

l: the twin sons of Jason and Hypsipyle, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypsipyle bears Jason twin sons resembling their father except in deceit, nearly sending them as messengers before fear of Medea stops her.

l: the marriage between Hypsipyle and Jason, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypsipyle and Jason’s chaste, legitimate marriage is publicly sanctioned and consecrated by Juno and Hymen; Hypsipyle later asks to remain Jason’s wife after his return.

l: Jason's voyage to Colchis and abduction of the maiden, Heroides and Amores
s: Jason’s voyage takes him from Lemnos to the lands associated with the Golden Fleece, where he completes the trials involving Mars’s bulls, the earth-born warriors, and the dragon. After the voyage he returns safely to Thessaly, but he does not return to Hypsipyle as promised.

Medea’s magic comprises incantations, enchanted herbs, songs, rites, curses, and powers over natural things. It is said to win and control Jason, protects him from fire-breathing bulls and armed warriors, and puts the sleepless dragon to sleep so he can take the Golden Fleece. Later, Medea says these arts no longer help her and prepares poison for Creusa.

l: the pregnancy and birth of twins, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypsipyle’s twin birth, caused by Jason: after he leaves knowing her pregnancy and hoping the child lives, Lucina aids delivery; Hypsipyle identifies the sons as both parents’ pledges.

Dido, also identified as Elissa Sychaei, is queen and founder of Carthage after exile, ruling a kingdom she offers Aeneas. Sister to Anna and Pygmalion, she receives Aeneas when he is cast ashore and loves him despite his faithlessness, hoping for wedlock and possibly carrying his child. As he prepares to leave, she writes pleading for a little time to calm her love and sorrow and learn endurance. Fearing abandonment, wounded by cruel love, she threatens and prepares to die by her sword.

Aeneas, a Trojan and Dardanian leader, is the son of Venus and Anchises and father of Ascanius, called Iulus. Carrying his aged father as a filial burden, he seeks Italy without knowing its location. Though Carthage offers a new city, walls, power, and love, he is determined to leave Dido; she calls him ungrateful, faithless, and deceptive, saying his refusal to delay gives cause and sword for her death.
Carthage is a newly founded, expanding city whose broad, envied walls, kingdom, peoples, wealth, and power rise as Dido offers it to Aeneas instead of Italy.

is_sought_by Aeneas [as a future kingdom] Italy is the destination Aeneas pursues, although Dido says he does not know where its kingdoms are and may reach the desired land only as a stranger, perhaps in old age.

l: Dido and Aeneas's love affair, Heroides and Amores
s: Dido and Aeneas’s love affair begins in a rain-driven cave through Venus’s influence, then ends in Dido’s enduring love, shame, and accusations of Aeneas’s faithlessness.

l: Aeneas's departure from Carthage, Heroides and Amores
s: Aeneas's imminent departure, driven by fate in his justification, is delayed by storms as Dido urges him to stay, offering herself and Carthage.

Dido's suicide is her impending death, which she presents as caused by Aeneas's departure and refusal. Writing beside a Trojan sword, she says Aeneas provides both the cause and the weapon, watches tears fall on it, tells Anna she will soon make final offerings to her ashes, and expects Aeneas to be named its cause.
Aeneas's fleet is shattered and only half refitted, causing a short delay.
A Trojan blade lies ready in Dido's lap; tears fall on its drawn steel, and she says it will soon be stained with blood instead of tears.

l: faithlessness and broken promises, Heroides and Amores
s: is_committed_by Aeneas [against Dido] Dido accuses Aeneas of abandoning her, breaking his pledge, and repeating the deception he practiced before. She warns that the sea exacts punishment for faithlessness, especially when love has been wronged.

The sea breaks on African shores and controls passage, at times granting and denying the way. It may prevent Danaans from returning or bar their fleet, yet fails to stop Protesilaus’s departure; it becomes a source of fear and separation as Laodamia watches it.
Dido's letter asks Aeneas to delay his departure and warns that she will die if he refuses. It describes her tears, the sword in her lap, and the fate she intends to bring about.
Dido says that, if Aeneas does not yield, her purpose is fixed to pour forth her life. She says that he cannot be cruel to her for long.
Dido says that her love must grow calm and that time and habit may teach her to endure her sorrow. She also says that her heart already bears the wound of cruel love.
Dido asks for time to learn to endure her sorrow bravely. Her tears fall onto the drawn sword as she writes.
Dido threatens suicide unless Aeneas grants a delay, then dies by her own hand with a sword; her death is recorded on a marble tomb inscription.

Hermione, Menelaus’s daughter and Orestes’s established wife, is forcibly held by Pyrrhus despite a prior promise. After calling on Orestes for protection, she laments her captivity, rejects Pyrrhus, affirms Orestes’s worth, and longs to be reunited with him.

Orestes is Agamemnon's son, Hermione's husband and kinsman, and an avenger of his father. He kills Aegisthus in revenge, yet is called a bad avenger for taking vengeance on his mother. Hermione later urges him courageously to reclaim her.
The Greeks are portrayed as possessing a large force that might pursue Helen if she is taken away. Paris nevertheless argues that their power will not necessarily prevail against Asia and Troy.

l: abduction of Hermione, Heroides and Amores
s: Pyrrhus abducts Hermione, holding and dragging her into his palace; disheveled, she compares herself to other captive women and asks Orestes for rescue.

l: marriage of Hermione and Orestes, Heroides and Amores
s: Hermione says that Tyndareus gave her to Orestes and that their marriage harmed no one. She maintains that marrying Pyrrhus would injure Orestes, and she declares that she will either die young or become Orestes' wife.

l: abduction of Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: is_comparable_to Theseus [Paris invokes Theseus's earlier abduction of Helen] Paris proposes that Helen leave with him for Troy, either willingly or as someone carried away. He argues that other women have previously been taken without their lands being attacked and tells Helen not to fear that her removal will inevitably lead to war.

l: Tantalid family curse, Heroides and Amores
s: A hereditary fate repeatedly leaves Tantalid women vulnerable to abduction, causing grief, loss, and disrupted marriages; Hermione believes it has pursued the family through her generation.

Deianira is an Aetolian woman, wife of Hercules and sister of Meleager, Tydeus, and Gorge. Jealous and distressed by Iole’s arrival, she sends Hercules a poison-smeared cloak, causing his death; guilt then drives her to resolve on suicide.

Hercules is a hero, son of Jupiter and husband of Deianira, whose long labours arise from Juno’s hostility. He conquers Oechalia, protects earth, bears the Nemean lion, supports Atlas, and is subjugated by Omphale. After conquering Oechalia, he is said to submit to Iole; Deianira hears he is dying from a poisoned cloak.
Iole is Eurytus’s captive daughter, publicly brought through the city after Oechalia’s fall; loved by Hercules, she becomes the figure Deianira fears will replace her.
Oechalia, a place, is conquered and falls to Hercules; Deianira fears Iole’s proud display may make it seem to stand again.

are_imposed_by Juno [an unending series of labours] Hercules's labours are described as a long series of victories over monsters and enemies, including the serpents, the Nemean lion, the Hydra, Geryones, Cerberus, and others. Deianira argues that love and Iole have overcome the man whom these labours could not defeat.
Lydian queen and Hercules's mistress, she makes him submit, wear women's clothing, and perform wool-working, taking his glory.

is_a centaur [a half-man who dies in the river Euenus] Nessus was defeated by Hercules and died in the Euenus after being struck by an arrow. Before dying, he told Deianira that his blood possessed the power of love.

l: Nessus's poisoned blood, Heroides and Amores
s: poisons poisoned cloak [the cloak is smeared with it] Nessus's blood was said to have the power of love after he was wounded. Deianira used it to treat the textile that she sent to Hercules.

l: Nessus's poisoned robe, Heroides and Amores
s: causes Hercules's death [through its poisonous substance] The cloak treated with Nessus's poison was sent by Deianira to Hercules. Rumour then reports that Hercules is dying from the poison in the garment.

results_in Iole [Iole is brought as a captive] Oechalia's fall is treated as one of Hercules's recent military achievements. Its conquest has led to Iole's captivity and to Deianira's fear that Iole will become Hercules's wife.

l: Hercules and Iole's proposed marriage, Heroides and Amores
s: Hercules and Iole's proposed marriage is a feared, shameful union: Deianira worries Iole will move from mistress to wife and replace her.

l: Deianira's grief and jealousy, Heroides and Amores
s: Deianira grieves over Hercules's absence, his new love, and the sight of Iole displayed as a captive. Her jealousy turns to horror and guilt when she learns that the gift she sent may be killing him.

is_caused_by poisoned cloak [the poison comes from Nessus's blood] Hercules's death is reported to Deianira as she writes, with the poisoned cloak blamed for his suffering. She imagines him being torn apart on Oeta and fears surviving as the cause of his death.

Deianira repeatedly asks why she delays dying and declares that her death will be the pledge of her marriage to Hercules. The unit ends with her farewell, but it does not state that she has yet killed herself.
is_part_man_and_part_bull hybrid The Minotaur is described as the creature that was part man and part bull. Theseus killed it with a club, after which Ariadne’s thread showed him the way out.

l: Ariadne's abandoned island, Heroides and Amores
s: An island surrounded by sea, empty of humans and cattle; Ariadne sees no ships or sailors and fears dangerous animals or hostile men may be there.

has_sails sails of Theseus's ship Theseus’s ship carries him away from Ariadne while she remains on the shore. Ariadne says that no other ship is available to carry her away and begs Theseus to turn it back.

l: sails of Theseus's ship, Heroides and Amores
s: are_carried_by winds [away from Ariadne's island] Ariadne sees Theseus’s sails filled by the south wind and watches them disappear from sight. She raises a white veil on a long branch so that Theseus might see a signal from the shore.

l: thread given to Theseus, Heroides and Amores
s: Ariadne gave Theseus a thread to guide his steps and show him the way back through the Labyrinth. She recalls that the thread was repeatedly taken up and passed through her hands.

is_described_as winding halls [where Theseus faced death] The Labyrinth is described as a winding structure containing stone halls and uncertain paths. Theseus escaped from it after Ariadne supplied the guiding thread.

l: bed shared by Ariadne and Theseus, Heroides and Amores
s: A bed shared by Ariadne and Theseus before her abandonment; Ariadne repeatedly returns, touching Theseus-warmed impressions and coverings and pleading for their return.

Aeolus is Canace's hard-hearted father and the grandfather of her infant son. As sovereign of the winds, he rules Boreas and controls East-winds in skins for Odysseus. His wrath dominates the account: he exposes Canace's secret, orders her infant abandoned, and sends her a sword as a death sentence.

l: Theseus's victory over the Minotaur, Heroides and Amores
s: is_attributed_to Theseus [after the Minotaur's defeat] Theseus’s victory involved killing the man-and-bull creature and escaping the winding stone passages. Ariadne says that she does not wonder that Theseus won because his chest was harder than stone.

l: Ariadne's abandonment by Theseus, Heroides and Amores
s: is_caused_by Theseus [while Ariadne slept] Theseus abandons Ariadne on the shore while she sleeps, taking his ship without her. Ariadne searches, calls, and signals for him, then faces isolation, exile, and the possibility of death.

l: Ariadne's aid to Theseus, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a assistance [enabling Theseus to navigate the Labyrinth] Ariadne aided Theseus by giving him the thread that directed him through the Labyrinth and enabled his return after he killed the Minotaur. She says that she does not demand gratitude for saving him, but argues that she should not be punished with death.

l: Ariadne's anticipated death, Heroides and Amores
s: Ariadne anticipates many possible deaths, including being killed by beasts, strangers, or a sword, and says that death would be less painful than waiting for it. She fears dying without her mother’s tears, without someone to close her eyes, and without burial rites.

l: marriage pledge between Ariadne and Theseus, Heroides and Amores
s: Theseus pledges Ariadne lifelong union, but while both live Ariadne says she is not his and the pledge is empty.

Canace, Aeolus's daughter and Macareus's sister and lover, secretly bears their infant son. After Aeolus discovers the relationship, she loses the child and receives a sword as punishment. Preparing to die, she writes Macareus, recounts their love and resolves to follow their son in death.

Macareus, Canace’s brother and lover, fathers their infant son, helps Canace in childbirth, promises marriage, and is asked after their deaths to gather the child’s scattered remains, bury them with Canace, and remember her.

l: Canace and Macareus's infant son, Heroides and Amores
s: Canace and Macareus's child, Aeolus's grandchild, survives attempts to remove him before birth and Canace's difficult labor, but Aeolus orders his exposure to wild beasts.

Canace's nurse, a caregiver, first recognizes Canace and Macareus's love, then helps conceal Canace's pregnancy, tries herbs and medicines to remove the child, and disguises the infant to carry him past Aeolus.

l: Canace and Macareus's incestuous love, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a forbidden relationship [between siblings] Canace and Macareus love each other as brother and sister but also as lovers. Their relationship leads to Canace's pregnancy, childbirth, public disgrace, and the deaths threatened or caused by Aeolus's punishment.

l: Canace's pregnancy and childbirth, Heroides and Amores
s: is_concealed_by sacrificial ritual disguise [devised by Canace's nurse] Canace's pregnancy is secretly concealed, and the nurse unsuccessfully tries to remove the child with herbs and medicines. After nine risings of Phoebus's sister and ten risings of the moon, Canace gives birth in severe pain while Macareus supports her.

l: the infant's attempted exposure and killing, Heroides and Amores
s: is_ordered_by Aeolus [the infant is to be abandoned to animals] Aeolus discovers the infant and orders him to be thrown to dogs and birds in a solitary place. The child cries and seems to entreat his grandfather, but he is carried into the forests to be devoured by mountain wolves.
Canace receives Aeolus's sword and says that she will bury the paternal gift in her breast. She declares that she will follow her infant's shade and will soon be neither called a mother nor bereaved.

is_written_by Canace [to Macareus] Canace's letter is written with a pen in her right hand while her left hand holds a drawn sword. She warns that its writing may be stained by her blood and uses it to tell Macareus about her suffering, her infant son, and her final wishes.

l: sword sent by Aeolus, Heroides and Amores
s: is_sent_to Canace [as a command to understand and perform her punishment] Aeolus's guard delivers Canace a sword and says that Aeolus sends it so she can understand what it means according to her desert. Canace accepts it as her father's gift and intends to use it against herself.

l: death and grief, Heroides and Amores
s: Canace grieves over the infant's exposure and expected destruction, lamenting that she cannot perform the usual rites or kiss his cold lips. She anticipates her own death and asks Macareus to gather the child's remains, bury them with her, and mourn over her wounds.
Creon’s daughter and Jason’s new bride in Corinth, Creusa becomes Medea’s threatened victim, doomed by prepared flames and poison.

l: the wedding of Jason and Creusa, Heroides and Amores
s: Jason and Creusa’s marriage is celebrated with Hymen’s song, torches, music, and Jason’s gold-led procession; Medea grieves, resolves vengeance, and Jason orders her exile.

l: the exile of Medea, Heroides and Amores
s: Medea's exile begins when Jason orders her to leave the Aesonian palace. She departs with their two children and with her love for Jason, after having already abandoned her kingdom, homeland, family, and home.

A wife and mother of two who brought her husband a golden ram, Grecian youth, and her aid in saving and advancing him. She humbly appeals for restoration of their marriage, invoking her service and children, but ends by warning that her rising anger threatens grave consequences.

Medea's husband, father of their children, once repeatedly sought his wife's aid; she says she saved his life, but now begs him to return, keep promises, and repay her despite his powerful new marriage.

l: children (Medea's and Jason's), Heroides and Amores
s: Two shared children closely resemble their husband; their appearance moves their mother to tears as she fears a cruel stepmother will mistreat them.

l: stepmother (the children's future stepmother), Heroides and Amores
s: is_cruel_to children (Medea's and Jason's) [as a hard stepmother toward them] The stepmother is portrayed as a hard and cruel woman who will be savage toward the speaker's children.
is_dowry_of speaker (Jason's wife) [the collective youth of Greece] The Grecian youth are presented as another part of the speaker's dowry.
Jason's wife asks her husband to restore the marriage bed, for which she says she madly abandoned much.

The speaker says that her dowry consists of the golden ram, the Grecian youth, and her husband safe and alive. She also declares that his survival, prosperity, and power to be ungrateful are hers by right.

l: anger of the speaker, Heroides and Amores
s: contains mighty threats [described as being in travail with them] The speaker's anger is said to be preparing great threats. She says that she will follow wherever her anger leads.

l: punishment threatened against the husband, Heroides and Amores
s: is_foretold by the speaker [the speaker says it is pointless to predict it in advance] The speaker indicates that punishment is imminent but refuses to predict its form, saying that it is not worth announcing the penalty because her anger is already producing mighty threats.
Laodamia, Protesilaus’s wife from Phylace, writes from Thessaly after his departure, grieving anxiously, praying and dreaming of him, and urging his safe return.
Haemonian lord of Laodamia, Protesilaus leaves her to travel with the Danaans, joins Greek forces at Troy, while she fears battle and urges his safe return.

l: Protesilaus's departure for Troy, Heroides and Amores
s: Protesilaus’s departure for Troy is delayed by wind at Aulis, then his ship leaves before Laodamia can finish speaking; his threshold stumble is taken as an unfavorable omen.

l: the fatal first landing at Troy, Heroides and Amores
s: is_predicted_by the prophecy [to kill the first Danaan who reaches Troy] A prophecy marks an unnamed person for an unjust fate as the first of the Danaans to touch Trojan soil. Laodamia fears that she will be the first woman to mourn her husband and prays that Protesilaus will not be eager or early.
A wind carries Protesilaus from Laodamia and favors Danaans; later contrary winds delay their ships, a divine delay Laodamia sees as intentional.

l: Laodamia's love and anxiety, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a emotional state [caused by separation and the war] Laodamia's faithful marital love causes her grief, sleeplessness, tears, prayers, and fear whenever she thinks of Troy, the winds, or the sea. Her longing also fills her imagined reunion with kisses, embraces, and hopes that Protesilaus will return safely.

l: wax image of Protesilaus, Heroides and Amores
s: is_treated_as Laodamia's husband [in Protesilaus's absence] Laodamia keeps a wax image that reproduces Protesilaus's features while he is away at war. She speaks affectionate words to it, embraces it, holds it in place of her real husband, and imagines that giving it a voice would make it Protesilaus.
Laodamia’s letter to Protesilaus recounts his departure, grief, anxious dreams, and war warnings, then vows to follow him whether he survives or dies and urges him to protect himself.

Hypermestra, Danaus’s pious daughter, is confined after faithfully refusing to kill Lynceus. Fearful, she warned him to flee and remains unrepentant, valuing filial duty and hands free from bloodshed.

is_a son of Aegyptus [the one brother left alive] Lynceus is the one son-in-law left alive after the massacre. Hypermestra wakes him, tells him to escape while night remains, and asks him either to rescue her or to kill and bury her if he cares for his pious sister.
Danaus is a mythic king and father of the Danaids, including Hypermestra. He orders brides to kill their husbands, counts the dead, and violently imprisons Hypermestra when Lynceus survives.
Danaids, fifty daughters of Danaus, enter bridal chambers armed; all but Hypermestra obey a command to kill their husbands, while she refuses.

l: the sons of Aegyptus, Heroides and Amores
s: are_bridegrooms_of the Danaids [they are massacred on their wedding night] The sons of Aegyptus marry the daughters of Danaus, but they are killed in the bridal chambers while asleep from food, wine, and the soporific drink. Lynceus is the sole survivor among them.

l: the prison (where Hypermestra is held), Heroides and Amores
s: holds Hypermestra [as a prisoner] The prison holds Hypermestra after she is dragged away from Danaus's feet. She writes from there with her hand weakened by the weight of her chains and by fear.

is_given_by Danaus [as the weapon for the commanded killing] Danaus gives Hypermestra a paternal sword for the killing. She raises it three times and brings it to Lynceus's throat, but her fear and piety prevent her from using it.
bind Hypermestra [heavy] Heavy chains bind Hypermestra in the house and later hinder her writing. Their weight causes her hand to fall, while fear further weakens her strength.

l: the soporific wine, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypermestra gives Lynceus wine that makes him sleep. When she wakes him, she identifies the drink as the cause of his sleep and gives him the opportunity to escape.

Hypermestra's letter recounts the wedding night, her refusal to kill Lynceus, his escape, and her imprisonment. She ends by asking Lynceus either to help her or to kill and bury her, but the chains and fear prevent her from writing more.

is_marked_by the wedding torches [the rites are unholy] The wedding takes place amid golden lamps, unwilling altar fires, and cries to Hymen. The bridegrooms enter the bridal chambers joyfully, though Hypermestra calls those chambers their tombs.

l: the massacre of the bridegrooms, Heroides and Amores
s: The Danaids kill the sleeping sons of Aegyptus during the night; by dawn, Danaus finds Lynceus alone escaped as Hypermestra confirms the dying groans.

l: Hypermestra's refusal to kill Lynceus, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypermestra refuses Danaus's commanded killing of Lynceus: she raises a paternal sword to his throat, but fear, piety, filial duty, and tenderness stop her.

occurs_in the prison (where Hypermestra is held) [under heavy chains] Hypermestra is imprisoned after Danaus discovers that Lynceus survived. She presents her imprisonment as the punishment for piety and says that she does not regret the act for which she was condemned.

is_enabled_by Hypermestra [she warns him to flee] Hypermestra tells Lynceus to flee while the dark night permits it. He wakes, sees the weapon in her trembling hand, and escapes while she remains behind.

l: piety and filial duty, Heroides and Amores
s: Hypermestra treats her refusal to kill Lynceus as an act of piety and faithfulness rather than a crime. She says that she would rather be accused of guilt than please her cruel father by committing murder.

l: guilt and repentance, Heroides and Amores
s: is_rejected_by Hypermestra [she does not regret remaining faithful] Hypermestra rejects repentance for sparing Lynceus and says that she does not regret being pious. She wishes repentance for the crime on Danaus and her cruel sisters, since wicked deeds are followed by such outcomes.

Sappho is a slight, dark-complexioned Lesbian woman, Pelasgida, poet, singer, and vates, renowned across every land and associated with a lyre and great poetic genius. She loves Lesbian women and passionately loves Phaon. In his absence, grief impedes her art until she feels bereft of genius. Writing to him, she recalls intimacy, neglect, family hardships, and her daughter, begs him to return, and concludes that, if he will not, she will seek escape from passion by leaping from the Leucadian cliff into death.

Phaon is a young, beautiful man, praised by Sappho for a face, youth, kindness, and poetic genius that inspire her powers. Once her lover, he leaves her tears and kisses behind, departs toward the women of Sicily, and delays returning. Sappho portrays his heart as churlish and unmoved: his absence has taken away what others admired in her, while his return could restore her poetry; she fears he may cause her death.

Ovid is a Paelignian poet from Sulmo, identified as Naso and author of The Amores, Heroides, and books of verse. His defining work is love elegy: he writes of Corinna and other beloved women, gives women fame through poetry, and regards poetry as both his wealth and a source of enduring reputation. Compelled and guided by Amor or Cupid, he portrays himself as a lover, even a slave to a woman, unable to govern himself or stop desiring what he also hates. Across the poems, his love life moves through pursuit, frustration, jealousy, injury, and reflection. He secretly approaches a door with wine and a fallen chaplet, begs a janitor for entry, threatens the house, and leaves refused, ashamed, and regretful of striking his mistress. He overhears Dipsas coaching a young woman, resents the power of poems as gifts, and curses Dipsas. He sends Corinna tablets through Nape, living on hope for a night with her. He accepts dependence on his mistress and even wants her husband to guard her more closely so that obstacles may sustain desire. He courts a woman at the circus, denounces the gods when a faithless girl breaks an oath without losing her beauty, and is delayed by a swollen river while rushing to his lady-love. He mourns Tibullus and questions piety and the gods, while asserting that poetry endures. Love and hate remain in conflict: he claims release from love but cannot cease loving. Visited by Elegy and Tragedy, he postpones greater work to continue short love poems. At the end, he regrets making Corinna common by praising her beauty, celebrates his standing as a poet, closes the elegies, and turns toward a greater subject associated with Lyaeus.

l: Sappho and Phaon's love, Heroides and Amores
s: Sappho and Phaon's love, remembered through intimacy and shared resting places, becomes unrequited after Phaon's departure, driving Sappho to seek release through the Leucadian leap.

Sappho’s poetry is lyric verse, turning to elegy when grief demands tears rather than lyre music. Inspired by the daughters of Pegasus, it unfolds from mourning to claims of sweet song, worldwide fame, and comparison with Alcaeus.

The Leucadian cliff is a high cliff in Ambracia, watched by Phoebus over the Aetian and Leucadian sea. Its deadly waves and rocks permit leaps that, under local mythic law, free sufferers from love: Deucalion did so. A Naiad directs Sappho there, though she prefers Phaon’s aid to its wave.

is_a leap from the Leucadian cliff [a remedy for unrequited love] The Leucadian leap is presented as a possible cure for Sappho's unrequited love. Sappho resolves to make the leap, asks the breeze and Love to support her, and intends afterward to dedicate her lyre to Phoebus.
Sappho's lyre, an Aeolian instrument, falls mute with its plectra silent in grief during Phaon's absence, turning away Lesbian women who come to hear it.
Phaon’s ship has sails and votive gifts prepared for its stern; Sappho urges its release toward Actian shores, imagining Cupid guiding it and its sails.
Sappho asks that at least the letter tell her, if Phaon has fled far away, that she should seek the fate offered by the Leucadian waters.

restores poetic genius [Sappho's poetic powers return with Phaon] Sappho repeatedly urges Phaon to return. She says that the return of Phaon will also bring back her poetic voice and asks him to make his ship's votive offering if he intends to come back.

is_associated_with Leucadia [through the Leucadian waters] Sappho fears that she may die and asks whether Phaon can bear the title of having caused her death. She contrasts death by falling from the rocks with the better possibility of joining her breast to Phaon's.
silences lyre [and the plectrum] Grief obstructs Sappho's artistic abilities and stops her former strength in song. It makes her plectrum and lyre silent.

receives_power_from Phaon [and loses its powers with him] Sappho says that her poetic genius has halted because of her troubles. She says that Phaon gave her genius its strength and has taken that strength away.

connects Sappho [to Lesbian women] Sappho recalls that she loved the Lesbian women to her reproach, but says that Phaon has taken away everything they once found pleasing in her. She nearly calls him 'my Phaon.'

torments Sappho [by postponing Phaon's return] Sappho asks Phaon why he tears her heart with delay if he is preparing a votive offering for his ship's stern. She says that returning promptly would suit him better if he had a feeling heart.

l: Paris's voyage to Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: uses Paris's fleet [built from Trojan and Idaean timber] Paris builds and equips a ship from the woods of Troy, sails from the Sigean shore with Venus's favor, and reaches the lands of Lacedaemon. His parents and Cassandra try to delay his departure, but he proceeds because he seeks Helen.

l: Paris and Helen's love, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris and Helen's love is a fierce, enduring, consuming passion, described as a deep wound from a heavenly arrow and as a newly begun feeling between them. Paris's desire begins through Helen's fame and Venus's promise, intensifies when he sees her, and drives him to travel, toil, declarations, and visible suffering over her closeness with Menelaus; he says only his funeral pyre will end it. Helen doubts the faith of his words but recognizes his signs, writing, affection, and hardships. She admits they are mutually drawn through beauty, nights, conversation, and shared dwelling, yet urges resistance before their fresh flame grows beyond control or fades as quickly as it began.

l: marriage between Paris and Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris seeks marriage with Helen, whom Venus promised him and whose image sponsors his ship. Valuing her above kingdoms and rewards, he asks her to marry him, claiming a future ceremony will correct her abduction and promising oaths and his kingdom.

l: Paris's letter to Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris’s letter to Helen declares his love, offering promised gifts and urging her to accept his proposed abduction. It opens with a greeting and confession, explains his journey, divine promise, and first sight of Helen, then asks her not to disappoint his hopes. Helen finds it dishonoring yet replies, noting its lavish gifts and appeal to abandon honor.

Helen's beauty is exceptionally powerful, whiter than snow and milk in Paris's view, and difficult to reconcile with chastity. In Paris's judgment of the goddesses, it surpasses Venus's promise and fame's reports, merits limitless adornment, and provokes his desire and jealousy.
Asia is a vast, wealthy land ruled by Priam, containing Ilion among innumerable cities; it has abundant men, horses, and resources rivaling the Greeks'.

l: Paris's proposed abduction of Helen, Heroides and Amores
s: threatens marital fidelity [by seeking a lawful wife] Paris's proposal is treated as an attempt to steal Helen a second time, after she had previously been seized by the Neptunian hero. Helen argues that her earlier abduction did not make her willing to be taken again and urges Paris not to pursue her or seek the disgraceful possession of her honor.

A voiceless page, written by Helen’s weary hand, carries and reveals her secret words; inexperienced, she entrusts it with an unusual office, then stops when tired, leaving Clymene and Aethra to speak the rest.

Adultery is a secret, difficult love pursued despite fear, scrutiny, locks, and guards. Helen feels invited to wrongdoing yet delays, fearing condemnation even from Paris, who shares responsibility. Its safety depends on the mistress’s guardian: cooperation, silence, false explanations, concealed messages, and invented visits protect the affair. Though doors and guards restrain bodies, desire remains unconfined, and adultery ultimately appears as a stain on the breast.

l: Helen and Paris's affair, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a secret relationship [conducted under Menelaus's absence] The affair is encouraged by Menelaus's absence, their mutual attraction, their conversations, the long nights, and their shared household. Helen insists that it must remain secret, warns that Paris is rushing too quickly, and postpones the private meeting he requests.

l: fame and public reputation, Heroides and Amores
s: Fame and public reputation are a burden: Paris’s praise heightens Menelaus’s suspicion, while Helen fears widespread reproach if she follows Paris. Reputation is harmed when infidelity is acknowledged; Ovid instead urges Corinna to seem modest, conceal sexual conduct, and preserve the belief in her faithfulness.

is_a burden [experienced by Helen] Fear makes Helen confused, conscious of public scrutiny, and hesitant despite her desire. She fears Menelaus's anger, Paris's possible infidelity, isolation in Troy, violence, the prophecies surrounding Ilion, and the consequences of being judged unfaithful.

Leander is a young man from Abydos, an Abydenus and swimmer who repeatedly crosses the sea to reach his beloved, Hero, guided by a light. Separated from her by the waters, he is defined by their love and by his boldness in overcoming the sea, even when boats face peril. In his letter from Abydos, a storm prevents him from crossing; he recalls earlier swims, takes strength from love, and intends to try again despite the danger. Others urge him to return to Hero but warn him not to trust his arms in a rough sea, suggesting he meet her halfway if necessary.

Hero, a Thracian girl and Maid of Sestos, lives in a tower across the sea from Leander, whom she loves as her sole delight and who loves her in return. Exceptional in beauty, tender and vulnerable, she waits through the nights, using a beacon to guide him and a spindle to endure the hours. She has welcomed him from the sea before, caring for his wet clothes and hair. In her letter, separation becomes unbearable: she confides in her nurse, fears another woman, blames the storm, and begs Neptune to let Leander return.
Abydos is Leander’s home and writing place, opposite Sestos across the Hellespont. Its people prevent his secret embarkation; Hero seeks travelers to ask after or write to her Abydos husband.
is_home_of Hero Sestos is Hero’s land and the destination of Leander’s crossings. Leander wishes either to be taken by Sestos or to have Hero taken by Abydos so that they may share one land.

The Hellespont is a swollen water and dangerous place, named after Helle because she drowned in it. It separates Abydos from Sestos and, for Leander and Hero, keeps the lovers apart while Leander repeatedly must swim across it. Stormy waves and winds make it hostile to Hero, threaten ships and swimmers, and determine whether the speaker may embrace the addressee. Hero watches and protests its waves, invokes Helle’s death, and kisses Leander’s garments before he crosses. Only when tranquil is swimming trusted.

The sea is a barrier between Leander and Hero, dividing the Hellespont’s two lands. Uncertain, swollen, rough, dark, wind-tossed, and stormy, it endangers ships and Leander’s swimming voyage. For a few nights it prevents and delays his crossing, despite prayers and Hero’s hope that it will calm; its waves beat the shores and dark clouds conceal daylight.

The storm is a violent, wind-produced disturbance of the sea that makes the waters turbulent. Hostile to Leander’s swimming voyage, it assails the sea, fights against his coming, and prevents him from crossing to Hero. Though Leander appeals to Boreas to calm the waters, the wind does not yield. After a gentler previous night, the sea quickly becomes storm-tossed, delaying and keeping him from Hero.
The letter, sent by Leander and carried by the seaman from Abydos to Hero, conveys his greetings and feelings; Hero receives, touches, and opens it.

Love is the force joining Leander and Hero in spirit and driving their secret, mutual relationship. It gives Leander strength, hope, and guidance as he crosses cold, dangerous water to reach Hero, yet makes separation more painful and may lead to his death if he fails. Their love is constrained by shame, fear of men's speech, delay, and uncertainty about faithfulness. Hero fears Leander’s affection may wander and wants their shared flame to endure. The whole moves from love’s uniting and motivating power through perilous crossing and anxious separation toward a hoped-for reunion and freedom from secrecy.

The speaker longs to embrace the addressee but is separated by a stormy sea. Driven by anxious love, he resolves to cross despite the waves and risk death, hoping either to reach the addressee’s arms or be cast ashore after shipwreck. He asks that a letter precede him only briefly, promising to follow soon.
The addressee is the speaker’s hoped-for refuge and shores, longed for yet perhaps unreachable; the speaker imagines a final embrace, tears, touch, and blame after death.

is_uncertain condition [together with the sea and wave] The wind is described as uncertain and potentially hostile. The speaker later wishes to be held by the winds while also being held by the addressee’s tender arms.
The speaker’s vessel seeks a suitable berth at the addressee’s shores, where it alone can stand securely and may remain.

l: crossing the sea, Heroides and Amores
s: The speaker intends to cross the sea even if it remains swollen for several nights and the waves are dangerous. He asks for only a short period of calm during the crossing and hopes to reach the addressee’s shore.

Death is portrayed as the feared possible end of anxious love, imagined in shipwreck and mourning. It is also prayed for as relief from the lover’s pain. Though it profanes sacred things, seizes worshippers and poets, and reduces Tibullus to an urn, it cannot wholly destroy poetry or the fame kept alive by song: after the final fire, a large part of the speaker endures.
The speaker hopes to be cast up on the addressee’s shores after shipwreck. He wants his ship to find a harbor there and wishes winter to remain once he reaches them.
A letter spends the night with the addressee for the speaker, while he prays to follow with minimal delay as straits impede the swimmer.

l: Leander's swimming voyage, Heroides and Amores
s: Leander's swimming voyage is a perilous attempt to cross the Hellespont to reach Hero. Stormy, dangerous seas hinder him, and Hero imagines his approach, considers meeting him in the water, and urges him to wait for calm conditions so he may arrive safely and embrace her.
Leander’s beloved maid fears for him while watching the waves, troubled by a dream of a drowned dolphin; believing her safety depends on his, she writes to him when the sea is impassable.

l: dream of the drowned dolphin, Heroides and Amores
s: A dream experienced before dawn depicts a dolphin swimming through wind-tossed waters, then cast onto thirsty sands where wave and life leave it. A girl fears its meaning, but a sacrifice wards against its threat and is considered to have cleared it.
In the girl's dream, dolphin swims through rough water, is cast onto thirsty sands, and dies as water and life abandon it.

Acontius is a wealthy, honorable lover and poet from Cea who loves Cydippe and seeks marriage as the fulfillment of what he regards as her pledged faith. Wounded by Love and jealous of a rival suitor or possible attendant, he uses deception to bind her: he writes a verse on an apple, causing her to pronounce an oath before Diana. In his letter he calls that single pledge sufficient, presents his ancestry and morals, asks Cydippe to reject her rival, and insists he seeks to be her husband rather than an adulterer. He petitions Diana for Cydippe’s welfare, fears for her affection and safety, and endures her anger, yet threatens force or further schemes if persuasion fails. Cydippe portrays his written oath as a distant wound that harms her, doubts his influence with Diana, but ultimately says she wishes to be united with him.

Cydippe is a maiden and virgin of marriageable age whose future is governed by an oath she unknowingly makes to Acontius. While traveling to Delos, she reads aloud the inscription on his apple without understanding its trap, thereby swearing before Diana to marry him. Although she is also intended for another husband in a marriage desired by her parents, she becomes bound to Acontius and fears Diana’s judgment if she breaks the pledge. Whenever marriage preparations arise, she suffers recurring illness, languor, wasting, fever, and weakness, and Hymenaeus flees her wedding rites. At first she protests that Acontius deceived an inexperienced girl and gained no glory by doing so; she writes to him pale and barely able to finish her letter. Yet she blushes at the oath, confesses that she wants to join him, rejects the intended husband, and tells her mother the circumstances. Her nurse protects her by concealing correspondence and signaling visitors. Her course moves from unwitting entrapment and illness toward acknowledging the pledge and accepting Acontius as husband.

Delos is a sacred island, stained with votive blood during sacrifice and visited by Cydippe. It contains Diana's lofty temple, other temples and porticoes, kings' gifts, statues, a horn-built altar, and the tree beside which the goddess gave birth; Cydippe recalls these holy sites and offerings.

Love is a cruel, powerful boy, Venus’s son and Mars’s stepson, with arrows, doves, and a chariot. It causes and strengthens Acontius’s passion, advises his binding of Cydippe through composed words, and sets nets for her. It also rules love poetry: interrupting an epic attempt, it steals a metrical foot, turns the work to elegy, shoots the speaker, and appears victorious with captives and attendants.

l: Cydippe's oath to Acontius, Heroides and Amores
s: Cydippe’s oath to Acontius is a disputed pledge of marriage made when Cydippe read aloud words on an apple Acontius threw to her in Diana’s temple. Acontius says Diana witnessed the binding oath and demands that Cydippe honor it rather than commit perjury. Cydippe argues that she did not swear freely: only deliberate intention makes words binding.

l: Cydippe and Acontius's marriage, Heroides and Amores
s: Cydippe and Acontius’s marriage is a promised but unfulfilled union. Acontius seeks marriage and pledged fidelity, claiming their oath binds Cydippe to him as her destined husband. As the marriage approaches, Cydippe’s illness repeatedly delays it; she questions whether her words were a deliberate promise that grants him marital rights.

Acontius’s letter is a second stratagem and evidence of his continued pursuit of Cydippe. It wounds the speaker from afar and contributes to her illness. Asking to be read so her illness may depart, it defends deception, invokes an oath, threatens further action, pleads for acceptance, and is answered by her confession that she wants union with him.

Cydippe’s illness is a persistent, unexplained languor that resists physicians and becomes severe whenever her marriage rites are prepared. It leaves her fevered, weak, wasted, bloodless, and pale, recurring as she attempts to evade a pledge. Its cause is disputed: some cite chance, divine disapproval, or Acontius’s arts, while Acontius says Diana sends it because Cydippe has broken her oath. He maintains that rejecting the rival suitor and honoring the pledge will restore her lasting health.

Acontius conceals a marriage oath on an apple and arranges for Cydippe to read it in Diana's temple, thereby ensnaring her without openly proposing. Cydippe condemns the attempted compulsion; Acontius admits deception, invokes love and union, calls his letter another stratagem, and threatens more.

causes violence against the mistress [by driving the lover to reckless blows] Anger makes the lover its prey and drives him to raise reckless hands against his mistress. Afterward, he recognizes that he used his strength against her and condemns his own anger.

Acontius’s apple is a rolling apple carrying a written oath and verse declaring his marriage claim. It comes or is thrown before Cydippe at Diana’s temple, where she reads its deceptive-looking but binding words in Diana’s presence and is caught into accepting the oath, nearly swearing again. Its bloodless color is compared with her pallor, and Acontius proposes a golden image at Delos as testimony that the inscription was fulfilled.

l: Cydippe's rival suitor, Heroides and Amores
s: Cydippe's rival suitor, promised her by her father, remains healthy while pursuing an unjust claim that causes her illness and danger; Acontius urges her to reject and bar him.

The letter urges Cydippe to fulfill her oath, explains the dangers of continued refusal, and tells her what to recount to her mother. Acontius closes it by asking her to act so that both of them may be safe.

l: the inscription on the apple, Heroides and Amores
s: An inscription presents Cydippe a marriage oath; read before Diana, it makes her blush and binds her to Acontius, though she says it forced or deceived her.

l: Cydippe's voyage to Delos, Heroides and Amores
s: Cydippe travelled by ship to Delos because she was eager to see the island, though the voyage began under an ill omen. She passed Myconos, Tenos, and Andros, reached Delos, and later visited its sacred places with her mother and nurse.

l: the rivalry between Acontius and Cydippe's suitor, Heroides and Amores
s: Acontius and Cydippe's suitor are engaged in a conflict in which neither yields and each believes the other is not his equal. Their rivalry obstructs both of their wishes, while Cydippe suffers the consequences.

is_a epistolary poem [in Ovid's Heroides] Heroides XXI is a letter in which a sick speaker addresses Acontius about his written oath, her failed marriages, Diana’s anger, and her eventual willingness to become his wife.

l: the written oath, Heroides and Amores
s: binds the speaker of Heroides XXI [through a written pledge] The written oath has bound the speaker despite her lack of genuine consent and has become the basis of her conflict with Acontius. She eventually yields to it and tells her mother about the pledge her tongue was trapped into giving.

l: the intended husband, Heroides and Amores
s: The intended husband honors the speaker’s virginity while sitting beside her, but her avoidance of touch, speech, and kisses makes him suspicious.
The Amores is a work of largely lighthearted love poems, featuring Corinna among several loves; it reflects Rome and Italy of its time and provides information on manuscripts and editions.

Corinna is a beautiful, celebrated, and haughty woman who is the speaker’s beloved and mistress, loved by Naso and Ovid and made the subject of verse. Her beauty is described as unmatched, but she lacks apparel or payment worthy of it; she knows the power of her appearance and gains pride from seeing herself in a mirror. She is watched by her husband, keeper, and guards, making access to her difficult, yet she also attracts wealthy lovers and is preferred by a newly rich soldier. Advice given around her urges the strategic use of modesty, rivals, refusals, and gifts. Her relationship with the speaker unfolds through desire, delays, jealousy, and public fame. She visits him at midday in a loose tunic, resists as he removes it, and they have sex before resting. At other times she hesitates to visit, sends tablets refusing him, keeps him out, and can renew his desire by feigning illness or wrongdoing before becoming affectionate. She is jealous of other women, especially Cypassis, and mourns her parrot, whose final word is her name. She suffers distress after losing her once abundant hair through her own treatment. She prepares for a dangerous sea voyage, and later undergoes a dangerous attempt to end a pregnancy, causing the speaker to fear for her life. Though Ovid says she first inspired his poetry, he fears his praise has made her common, known to many, and sexually available to others; another woman even claims the distinguished name Corinna because of that poetry.

Tibullus is a sacred bard and the glory of Elegy. He dies, is burned on a high funeral pyre, and is buried as ashes in an urn while his mother and sister mourn; Delia and Nemesis loved him. His fame endures, and he is imagined received in Elysium.

Love poetry is a light poetic form, suited to youthful subjects and the alternating six- and five-foot elegiac couplet, including The Amores. It begins when the speaker abandons violent epic after Cupid changes his meter, drawing its subject and lasting fame from the beloved woman. In the later account, Elegy and Cupid defend its power against Tragedy, and the poet continues it temporarily before a greater task.

l: P. Ovidius Naso, Heroides and Amores
s: P. Ovidius Naso is a poet, lover, and author of the Amores, revised from five booklets into three. In its episodes, the speaker suffers frustrated meetings, reproaches Aurora, comforts the beloved woman, and trusts poetry to preserve him after death. Recalling her apparent infidelity, he prays for death, threatens retaliation, then relents at her sorrow, asks for kisses, and remains jealous of a rival.

l: the poet's Amores, Heroides and Amores
s: A love-poetry work in elegiac couplets, now three booklets rather than five, presenting Cupid, Love, the speaker’s beloved woman, and Corinna.

l: the speaker's beloved woman's husband, Heroides and Amores
s: is_married_to Corinna [he is her husband] The beloved woman's husband attends the same banquet as the speaker and the woman. The speaker fears his physical intimacy with her, instructs her to avoid his embraces and kisses, and hopes that wine will make him sleep so that the lovers can find an opportunity to meet.

Love is a ruling, cruel power that takes possession of the speaker after Cupid’s wounding, enslaves lovers, and is neither idle nor spiritless. It demands experience and energy, drives hardship and action, causes sleeplessness, and directs Ovid from epic subjects toward elegies. It also divides the speaker’s affection between two beautiful women, yet he chooses love’s trouble over solitude and imagines an erotic death. From initial torment and resistance, its burden becomes lighter when accepted; it then grows through refusal, fear, delay, and obstacles, while excess makes it cloying and harmful.

l: the husband-wife banquet, Heroides and Amores
s: The husband-wife banquet brings the speaker, Corinna, and Corinna’s husband together; amid the crowd, the speaker secretly directs Corinna through touches, looks, gestures, cups, and wine while forbidding affection for her husband.

Cupid's triumph is imagined as a sacred public victory procession over lovers: Cupid rides a golden dove-drawn chariot while captives, attendants, roses, and jewels follow, ending with the speaker's submission as newly captured prey.

l: the speaker's submission to Cupid, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a submission [to Cupid's laws] The speaker confesses that he is Cupid's new prey and stretches out his hands to accept Cupid's laws. He asks for peace rather than war and accepts that his poetry must rise in six-foot lines and settle into five-foot lines.

The janitor, a door guardian at the mistress's threshold, is enslaved and chained. Iron-hearted toward the lover's pleas, he repeatedly refuses to open the door despite appeals to gratitude and threats, seeming suited to guard a gloomy prison.

is_a beautiful girl [whose threshold the janitor guards] The mistress is the lover's beloved and is inside the house whose door he cannot enter. In the later episode, she is frightened and wounded when the lover tears her hair and marks her cheeks, but she remains silent while her tears and expression accuse him.

A portal secured by a guardian and bar, braced with hard oak, stays closed and deaf to a lover’s tears, prayers, threats, and appeals. A seeming movement proves to be wind; the lover curses it and bids farewell to door and posts.
secures door [during the lover's vigil] The lover repeatedly orders the door bar to be removed before the night ends. It remains in place, braced by hard oak, and prevents him from entering.

is_long long [the janitor's burden of slavery] The chain binds the janitor, and the lover wishes that the janitor may eventually be freed from it and no longer have to drink the water of slavery. The chain is also invoked as a possible punishment for the lover's own violent hands.

encourages lover [with love and wine, toward lack of restraint] The night initially frightens the lover with darkness and empty phantoms, but Love makes him brave enough to travel and keep watch at the door. As the hours pass, the city becomes silent, dew falls, and dawn approaches while the door remains shut.

l: violence against the mistress, Heroides and Amores
s: Violence against the mistress is committed by the lover in madness: after threats and tearing her gown, he injures Corinna, whose fear and tears make him recognize his crime.

l: the lover's vigil at the door, Heroides and Amores
s: The lover spends the night outside the closed door, repeatedly calling for the bar to be removed and listening for signs that the door has opened. He sheds tears, wears a garland that falls from his hair, and remains outside until the approach of dawn, when he leaves the garland on the threshold as evidence of his miserable vigil.

Dipsas, whose thirst accords with her name, is an old bawd and practitioner of magic. Never sober in relation to Aurora, she knows Aeaean incantations and magic that can control clouds and day and summon dead ancestors. As a profaner of chaste union, she advises a young woman as a procurer, urging wealthy lovers, deception, rivalry, feigned feeling, and demands for gifts; the narrator overhears her.

l: the wealthy young lover, Heroides and Amores
s: A wealthy young lover, captivated by a young woman's face, desires her and can meet her needs; Dipsas urges her to profit from him while keeping him uncertain and jealous.

requires youth [the age suited to warfare is also suited to Venus] War is compared with love through their shared dangers, sleeplessness, watchfulness, sieges, attacks, and uncertain outcomes. The unit says that both war and love can bring down people who seemed impossible to defeat, while the defeated may rise again.

l: gifts and payment for sexual favors, Heroides and Amores
s: The topic is gifts and payment for sexual favors. Dipsas teaches a young woman to feign love, admit lovers according to their gifts, and use her slaves, sister, mother, and nurse to seek more, including through birthday pretexts, rivals' presents, and unrepaid loans; the narrator's poetry is deemed inadequate. The later account condemns payment as degrading and incompatible with love, distinguishing it from freely given gifts. It values a poor lover's service, devotion, faithfulness, and poetry, whose fame can outlast material gifts.
Isis is a goddess associated with Paraetonium, Canopus, Memphis, Pharos, and the Nile, invoked to attend to Corinna and grant her life, sparing her and the speaker.

The lover is a soldier in love: serving and guarding a mistress, watching rivals as enemies, and besieging her threshold. Former idleness becomes action under love. Suited to a spirit experienced in trials, the lover endures night, cold, rain, snow, mountains, rivers, and sea travel.

A warrior serves as a captain’s guard, keeping watch at the door and through the night. He endures long roads, harsh weather, and ground rest, scouts enemies, besieges cities, breaks gates, and embodies courage and endurance.
A woman who sells sexual access at a fixed price, the harlot is controlled by a greedy pander, curses that authority, and performs under compulsion for gain.

charges man [for mutual sexual pleasure] The woman is criticized for being the only creature said to demand payment for mutual sexual pleasure, to hire out her nights, and to profit from what both partners desire. The unit nevertheless says that a woman may properly request gifts from a wealthy person and that a poor lover should give whatever he has, including service, devotion, faithfulness, and poetry.

pays woman [for sexual pleasure] The man is presented as contributing to sexual pleasure together with the woman, yet being made to suffer a financial loss when the woman demands payment. A poor man is said to offer his service, devotion, faithfulness, and whatever possessions he has to his beloved.

is_mutual woman [shared by man and woman] Sexual pleasure is described as something that man and woman both enjoy and jointly produce. Because it is mutual, the unit questions why one person should sell it and the other should have to buy it.

Nape is a personal attendant, not a handmaid, skilled at arranging hair, giving signals, and aiding secret nighttime meetings. Faithful to Naso in trouble and touched by Cupid, she repeatedly urges Corinna to visit him. Naso ultimately entrusts her with tablets, asking her to secure Corinna’s response.

The wax tablets are double writing tablets with wax surfaces, inscribed by Naso and carried by Nape to Corinna as love correspondence. Naso asks Corinna for a reply, saying “Come!” would suffice and promising to dedicate them to Venus. They return bearing her refusal to come that day, provoking curses and wishes for their destruction.
A terse wax message asks Corinna to come secretly at night, saying Naso’s hope of seeing her keeps him alive and seeking a prompt reply.

l: secret nighttime meeting, Heroides and Amores
s: Nape is known for her usefulness in the service of a secret nighttime meeting and for giving signals. She has often encouraged Corinna to come to Naso, but the unit does not state that the meeting occurs.

Naso’s love correspondence with Corinna is carried through Nape and written on wax tablets. Naso wants Corinna’s written response to occupy the tablets rather than leave them largely blank, though he would accept the single-word reply “Come!”

The dawn ends the speaker’s night with the beloved woman even though sleep is still deep, the air cool, and the birds singing. Its arrival wakes travelers, soldiers, farmers, boys, lawyers, and women who work wool.

is_a fine and abundant bodily hair [formerly belonging to the beloved woman] The beloved woman’s former hair was abundant, delicate, easily arranged, and a mixture of black and golden color. It endured irons and fire but was ultimately ruined by her own dyes and treatments; the speaker says that replacement hair from captive German women will be sent.

Envy accuses the speaker of wasting his vigorous years and producing poetry instead of pursuing military prizes or legal work. The speaker says that Envy feeds on the living but becomes quiet after death.

l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores
s: Poetry and poetic fame are a powerful art that seeks lasting renown worldwide. Song can overcome natural and physical barriers, including barred doors, and earns the poet favor from his beloved mistress. It outlasts material achievements, rulers, wealth, monuments, and its creators, preserving named poets’ works and promising the speaker’s own survival through verse.

l: the beloved mistress, Heroides and Amores
s: A beloved woman initially closes her door to the poet, but song and poetry soften resistance; abandoning thunderbolt imagery for elegy, he gains her beauty, favor, and eventual return.

l: the mistress's guardian, Heroides and Amores
s: The mistress’s guardian is a eunuch who strictly blocks Ovid’s access to the beloved mistress. Unable to share mutual sexual love, he is urged to accept gifts, gain honor and savings through silence, permit secret meetings, and avoid punishment for exposing an affair.

The husband is Corinna’s jealous judge in accusations of adultery, yet is influenced by his beloved mistress and fails to guard her from the speaker. Criticized as slow and overly tolerant, he is urged to shut doors, investigate visitors and messages, and recognize her estrangement; his indulgence enables the affair and threatens the speaker’s possession of her.

is excessive vigilance [toward a mistress] Excessive guardianship is presented as provoking hatred and making illicit love more desirable. Ovid argues that surveillance damages the husband, mistress, and guardian, while a guardian who keeps silent gains influence, rewards, and eventual freedom.

The beloved girl, the speaker/lover’s mistress, secretly communicates with and kisses a rival despite shared kisses and instruction in kissing; confronted, she blushes and seems sorrowful, then gives the speaker/lover exceptionally pleasing kisses.

Love is a painful yet desired force: it makes the speaker pray for death, suffer jealousy over the beloved girl’s kisses, and feel physically weakened. It repeatedly draws him back into its wars and familiar weapons even when desire cools, while its uncertain pleasures and rejections outweigh peaceful rest. By the end, love affects mortals and gods alike and overcomes the speaker’s hatred of the beloved woman’s faults through her beauty.

The beloved girl’s infidelity is revealed not by intercepted letters or gifts but by the speaker/lover’s direct observation of her secret signs and kisses with another man. The speaker/lover considers his case against her overwhelmingly strong, yet wishes he could be unable to win it.

Jealousy makes the speaker/lover angry when he sees the beloved girl kissing another man, but it also torments him after she gives him better and seemingly newly learned kisses. He fears that the rival has tasted the same pleasures and wishes the rival’s kisses had not been equally satisfying.
Kisses shared with the beloved girl are intimate; after another man apparently teaches her, her kisses to the speaker become heartfelt, powerful, and more skillful.

The parrot comes from India and is prized for rare beauty, a Punic-red and saffron beak, human-voice mimicry, peaceful companionship, and a frugal diet of nuts, poppy-seeds, and water. After dying, it bids Corinna farewell, is mourned by birds and Corinna, joins pious birds in Elysium, and receives a body-sized tomb.
turtle-dove, a friendly, faithful bird, lives harmoniously as parrot’s companion, remains loyal through their shared life’s end, and is urged to grieve first.

Cypassis is Corinna’s skilled, faithful female servant and hairdresser. Accused of sharing Corinna’s couch with the speaker, she is first denied by him, then revealed as his secret partner; he threatens to expose their meetings if she refuses him.

l: the speaker's beloved, Heroides and Amores
s: A fair lady loved by Ovid receives and wears a welcome ring. The speaker imagines her touching herself, bathing, and sealing secret tablets with it, then urges her to come quickly by small carriage if she cares for him.

l: Cypassis and the speaker's affair, Heroides and Amores
s: is_secret stolen delight [between the speaker and Cypassis] The affair is a secret sexual relationship between Cypassis and the speaker. Although the speaker denies the accusation when defending himself to Corinna, he later refers openly to their previous encounters and uses knowledge of them to pressure Cypassis into another meeting.

l: two simultaneous love affairs, Heroides and Amores
s: are_experienced_by the speaker [at the same time] The speaker admits that he loves two women at the same time, despite having previously denied that this was possible. He presents this condition as shameful but acknowledges that he has been caught loving both simultaneously.
Corinna's voyage is a dangerous sea journey from home, exposed to adverse winds and storms; the speaker fears for her, urges her return, and hopes to welcome her safe escape.

has_as_spoil Corinna [captured by the speaker's strategy] The speaker claims a triumph because Corinna is in his arms after being guarded by her husband, keeper, and door. He calls it a special victory because it was won without bloodshed or military assistance, with himself serving as commander, soldier, cavalry, infantry, and standard-bearer.
Ilia, a Trojan descendant and Vestal, suffers distress from her uncle's crime and Mars's wrongdoing, fears disgrace, drowns herself in Anio's waters, and becomes Anio's wife.
Pregnancy is a hidden bodily burden that endangers Corinna; as she struggles to deliver, a speaker fearing responsibility begs Isis and Ilithyia to save her.

Abortion is condemned as self-destructive violence: women wound themselves and poison unborn children to avoid bodily marks, may die after destroying pregnancy, and are urged to let pregnancy reach natural maturity.

l: the unborn children, Heroides and Amores
s: The unborn children are vulnerable, tender lives in the womb, threatened by abortion, weapons, and deadly poisons; destroying them before birth prevents future people from existing.

A gift for the speaker’s fair beloved, the ring carries the giver’s love rather than material value. Sent to circle her finger, stay with her even in bathing, and seal secret letters, it becomes the speaker’s envied imagined means of touching her lips and bosom as a man.

Sulmo is a small, wholesome, fertile town in the Paelignian fields, watered by streams and enclosed by walls. It is Ovid’s hometown and the speaker’s setting; though its waters and fields are praised, it cannot please him while his beloved is distant.

l: Ovid's Paelignian homeland, Heroides and Amores
s: The Paelignian country is Ovid’s small, healthy, water-rich homeland, fertile in corn, grass, grain, grapes, olives, and the berry-bearing tree of Pallas. It begins as abundant, refreshed by streams and breezes; without the beloved it feels no longer healthy. Ovid then claims its people, their honorable arms, and his future glory.

l: the sea voyage and journey, Heroides and Amores
s: A speaker imagines a journey with his beloved: together they would cross the Alps, Libyan Syrtes, and dangerous seas without fearing Malea or Charybdis, and he would carry her if Neptune defeated their ship. It ends by contrasting Hero’s visitor’s failed, blinded route.

l: separation from the beloved, Heroides and Amores
s: separates Ovid [from the beloved] Separation places the speaker away from the woman who causes his passion. It makes Sulmo and his father's country seem like Scythia, the fierce Cilicians, the green Britons, and rocks reddened by Promethean blood. The beloved had sworn to remain his companion, but the speaker says that girls' promises are often carried away by wind and water.

l: love and longing, Heroides and Amores
s: The speaker's love is expressed through the gift of the ring and through his wish to become the object that touches and accompanies his beloved. His longing makes him envy his own gift and desire physical closeness with her. He asks her to turn her promises into actions by coming to him.

Beauty gives confidence, pride, and lasting privilege, even protecting a faithless girl from divine offense. Yet it breeds arrogance, jealous desire, and adultery; its possessors should not scorn lesser partners or let beauty promise rule.

The speaker values felicitous poems as more important than great wealth and says that many women want to acquire a name through his poetry. He declares that only his mistress will be sung in his books and that she alone will provide the cause for his poetic talent. Love redirects his poetry from epic and tragedy toward the art of love and letters written for legendary figures.

Elegy is a feminine, love-associated poetic genre personified as a graceful woman with uneven feet, thin robe, loving expression, and a myrtle branch. She inspires the poet, enables Corinna’s secret love, and defends her light Cupid-suited style, winning the poet’s continuation. She gives the poet’s love lasting renown, then mourns Tibullus with loosened hair and tears.

Tragedy is a Roman, exalted personified genre. She appears in a powerful stride with a royal sceptre and high Lydian buskin, reproaches the poet’s continual love writing, urges heroic poetry as greater work, then grants time for tender love poems.

l: woman at the races, Heroides and Amores
s: A woman attending circus races favors a charioteer while a poet beside her desires her, praises her appearance, seeks Venus’s aid, and reads her smile and eyes as promise of further favor.

A racing venue with assigned seating and a starting line, circus places the poet and woman close together, hosts four-horse chariot races and a gods’ procession, and lets its crowd demand restarts by waving togas.
